{"id": "12:35/q03", "question": "Who are 'them'?", "turns_on": "Whether the plural denotes the governing household or consultative entourage, one ruler spoken of collectively, or the wife's mixed group.", "positions": [{"id": "12:35/q03/p1", "position": "The Aziz or ruler and his household, advisers, or associates.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshaf and al-Nasafi name the ruler or minister and household; Abu Hayyan names the Aziz and household. Al-Tha'labi, al-Qurtubi, and al-Wahidi include officials or companions; al-Tabataba'i includes his wife, advisers and attendants. Study Quran reports both family and entourage readings. Al-Tabari explains how a singular actor can be referred to by a plural group, citing 3:173."}, {"id": "12:35/q03/p2", "position": "The king or Aziz alone, described by a plural because his decision involved consultation.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari compares a single speaker described as 'the people' in 3:173; Ibn Atiyya explicitly says the king alone with consultation. Al-Tabrisi favors the king despite the preceding women."}, {"id": "12:35/q03/p3", "position": "Zulaykha and her helpers or the wife's group of advisers and commanders.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi and Abu Ali allow a mixed group with masculine agreement; Ibn Ashur identifies the chief wife's advisers and commanders."}]}
{"id": "12:35/q04", "question": "What is the grammatical subject of 'badā'?", "turns_on": "Whether an entire oath sentence can be the subject of a verb, or an implicit noun/object and quoted speech must be supplied; the sources also transmit conflicting positions from Sibawayh.", "positions": [{"id": "12:35/q04/p1", "position": "An omitted noun for the newly appearing decision, opinion, or imprisonment is its subject; the following clause explains it.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj notes Arabic normally omits the understood badāʾ; Muhammad ibn Yazid and Abu Uthman supply an implicit noun or badw. Al-Mubarrad invokes a poem with omitted ḥaqq. Ibn Atiyya cites badw or raʾy; al-Kashshaf and al-Nasafi specify the decision; Abu Hayyan and al-Samin prefer imprisonment inferred from the threat or sijn, and al-Samin cites readings of al-sijn. Al-Mazini selects the first subject analysis in al-Alusi's account. Sibawayh is reported by Ibn Atiyya as rejecting a sentence as subject, although other transmitters attribute the opposite view to him."}, {"id": "12:35/q04/p2", "position": "The clause 'they will surely imprison him' itself serves as the subject.", "reasons": "Al-Farra presents the full clause as filling the subject position; al-Nahhas and al-Qurtubi report this from Sibawayh, whereas Ibn Atiyya reports Sibawayh explicitly rejecting it. Al-Samin ascribes it to Kufans. Al-Razi challenges the premise that a verb cannot be discussed as a subject, using ḍaraba fiʿl: treating the form as a noun would make the predicate 'verb' false. Al-Alusi cites 36:31 and 14:45 for a full proposition as subject but says most grammarians reject it. Ibn Ashur reports Hisham and Tha'lab permit clauses generally, while al-Farra and others permit them with cognitive verbs and suspension."}, {"id": "12:35/q04/p3", "position": "The oath clause is quoted speech after an omitted 'they said,' while an omitted decision or object belongs to 'badā'.", "reasons": "Abu Uthman compares an omitted 'they said' in 39:3. Al-Farra's parse supplies raʾy and qālū; Ibn Ashur treats the oath sentence as detached from badā and its omitted object as understood, an instance of suspension beyond verbs of thought according to Yunus ibn Habib. Al-Alusi reports an object of implicit saying or explanatory clause; Ibn Ashur says suspension fits better than a clause as subject."}]}
{"id": "12:35/q05", "question": "What signs had they seen?", "turns_on": "Which reported events count as evidence: the shirt and testimony directly exonerate Joseph, while several commentators dispute whether scratches or cut hands do.", "positions": [{"id": "12:35/q05/p1", "position": "The signs were proofs of Joseph's innocence, chiefly his shirt torn from behind, sometimes with the witness's judgment.", "reasons": "Mujahid names the rear tear; Ibn Jawzi transmits the shirt and cousin's judgment, and Ibn Atiyya says the shirt test is probative whether an infant's miraculous speech or an adult's inference. Abu Hayyan makes the same distinction. Al-Alusi reports Mujahid restricting the signs to the tear because the women's cuts are not proof; he also reports Qatada limiting the signs to the tear while treating the dual as plural. The witness's ruling and the wife's admission appear in al-Wahidi; Ibn Ashur says the proofs established Joseph's truth and her falsehood."}, {"id": "12:35/q05/p2", "position": "The signs included the rear shirt tear and the women's cut hands, often with further evidence.", "reasons": "Qatada, al-Suddi and many later sources give both. The additions vary: face scratches in al-Tabari and al-Tha'labi; the witness, awe or child's testimony in Ibn Jawzi, al-Qurtubi, al-Baghawi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi; the child's testimony and race to the door in al-Tabataba'i. Al-Alusi reports an argument that hand cuts show Joseph's beauty made the women likely initiators, while his resistance to them supplied a further sign. Al-Wahidi doubts the cuts prove innocence, as do Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan."}, {"id": "12:35/q05/p3", "position": "The signs included the shirt tear and scratch, bodily or knife marks.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas reports scratches on the woman's face in al-Tabari and marks on Joseph's body plus knife marks in al-Durr and al-Alusi. Ikrima reports the scratched face in Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Durr. Al-Razi adds the Aziz's verdict in 12:28 and says other decisive signs were hidden to cover the scandal. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan object that scratches themselves do not prove innocence."}, {"id": "12:35/q05/p4", "position": "The signs included the child's or nursing witness's speech and the shirt test.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd calls the nursing woman's courtyard statement a sign; al-Durr calls the speaker an infant. Al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi include the child's testimony; Bursavi and al-Tabataba'i add it to the rear tear, and al-Tabataba'i also mentions the race to the door. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan say infancy would make the testimony a miracle, whereas an adult's statement would be an inference."}, {"id": "12:35/q05/p5", "position": "The signs were Joseph's evident beauty and chastity, which made the women call him an angel.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi gives this as an alternative to shirt and hand cuts; Ibn Jawzi repeats it. Al-Qurtubi judges a 'blessings' interpretation less sound than signs of innocence."}, {"id": "12:35/q05/p6", "position": "The signs showed that the women had despaired of obtaining Joseph.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi reports this alternative interpretation."}, {"id": "12:35/q05/p7", "position": "The plural refers broadly to clear circumstances and perhaps unmentioned proofs of Joseph's innocence.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya says no single sign need be identified, and the proofs varied in degree; Abu Hayyan prefers several manifest proofs suggested by the plural, perhaps the witness's statement and unmentioned evidence. Al-Alusi likewise allows omitted prophetic signs."}]}
{"id": "12:35/q06", "question": "What decision did they make after the signs?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:35/q06/p1", "position": "They knowingly resolved to imprison innocent Joseph for a temporary, open-ended period, reversing an earlier plan to release or merely avoid him.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari says they reversed an apparent release; al-Zajjaj, al-Baghawi and Ibn Jawzi say the master had first ordered only that Joseph be ignored. Ibn Kathir says they judged confinement expedient despite proofs of chastity. Al-Tabari says they would decide their next course later. Al-Biqa'i emphasizes the injustice and folly; Islahi notes the Aziz's unrestricted power over an enslaved person and his office and rank in the royal guard made imprisonment easy. Al-Tabataba'i says firm resolve is expressed by the oath lām."}]}
{"id": "12:35/q07", "question": "How did the decision to imprison Joseph arise?", "turns_on": "Whether the initiative came from the wife's complaint, women's earlier plotting, or an adviser's counsel; these reports may describe stages of the same decision.", "positions": [{"id": "12:35/q07/p1", "position": "The wife accused Joseph of publicly disgracing her and demanded either freedom to defend herself or his imprisonment; the Aziz and advisers complied.", "reasons": "Al-Suddi, Wahb and later transmitters vary whether she asked to leave, defend herself, apologize, or be jailed as she had been confined. Ibn Atiyya says she framed the account after Joseph refused sin; al-Razi calls the accusation false. Al-Wahidi and Ibn Abi Hatim say she warned that people would believe Joseph if he stayed free. Al-Kashshaf, al-Alusi and Asad stress the husband's submission; Asad quotes Zamakhshari's image of the wife holding his camel's reins. Al-Wahidi and al-Qurtubi state he knew Joseph was innocent."}, {"id": "12:35/q07/p2", "position": "The women urged the wife to imprison Joseph, hoping isolation would let them entice him; when he resisted, she appealed to the master.", "reasons": "Wahb says their proposal also sought to stop public gossip that she hated Joseph; the master later treated him harshly."}, {"id": "12:35/q07/p3", "position": "An adviser urged imprisonment so the public would excuse the Aziz and blame the household if Joseph remained free to tell his story.", "reasons": "Al-Durr reports this from Ikrima."}]}
{"id": "12:35/q08", "question": "Why did they want Joseph imprisoned?", "turns_on": "The sources attribute overlapping aims to different actors: rulers' public reputation, public inference of guilt, the wife's desire to control Joseph, or a provisional wait.", "positions": [{"id": "12:35/q08/p1", "position": "To quiet gossip, conceal the scandal, protect the household's reputation, and s

eparate Joseph from the wife for a time.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi prefers this account; al-Razi says the Aziz sought to quiet scandal; Ibn Kathir calls it a conjecture and al-Suddi says her behavior would otherwise be exposed while Joseph's name was cleared. The wife feared discussion after the women dispersed, according to Ibn Ashur; Islahi says confinement could reduce her infatuation. Al-Tabataba'i also suggests avoiding disorder or wider infatuation with Joseph's beauty. Al-Kuranyolu says the household sought to conceal the affair."}, {"id": "12:35/q08/p2", "position": "To make the public believe Joseph was guilty because criminals are imprisoned.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi and al-Baydawi give the appearance of guilt as a motive; Bursavi assigns it especially to the wife. Ibn Ashur says the wife meant to conceal Joseph's innocence, and Islahi says people would infer he was punished. A report from Ikrima says an adviser expected blame to shift to the household if Joseph spoke freely."}, {"id": "12:35/q08/p3", "position": "The wife hoped prison would humble, punish, or coerce Joseph into yielding to her.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshaf gives both her possible loss of hope and her hope for submission; al-Qurtubi reports concealment and renewed desire or a plot to wear him down. Al-Nasafi, Bursavi, al-Alusi, al-Tabataba'i, Asad and Kuranyolu state variants of her coercive purpose. Al-Tabrisi reports the prison was near her so she could see him from her window."}, {"id": "12:35/q08/p4", "position": "They meant to observe Joseph's behavior and decide their next course later.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari says the decision was provisional; al-Baydawi says they would see what happened; al-Kashshaf and Abu Hayyan connect the term to what the wife would see Joseph do."}]}
{"id": "12:35/q09", "question": "How does 'they will surely imprison him' fit grammatically after 'badā'?", "turns_on": "Whether the oath force is supplied by implicit speech or an interrogative setting, and whether emphatic nūn can occur after a question.", "positions": [{"id": "12:35/q09/p1", "position": "It is the response to an unspoken oath, introduced through an implicit statement of their resolve.", "reasons": "Al-Farra says the lām works after expressions of speech, opinion, or knowledge and cites 12:26, 12:36, 12:80. Al-Tabari's rejecting grammarians say emphatic nūn does not follow a plain question. The Kufan explanation lets badā carry 'they said/decided'; al-Samin says the majority posit implied speech. Al-Alusi allows an implied saying or explanatory clause. Al-Tabataba'i calls the lām an oath of firm resolve, and Ibn Ashur treats the oath clause as suspended from badā. Sībawayh says a positive oath about an unfulfilled action takes lām and either light or heavy emphatic nūn, and verbs with oath force such as 'I swear' and 'I testify' license the construction. Al-Khalīl says nūn distinguishes the future oath from ongoing action, preventing ambiguity with a negative oath, and treats nūn as attached to lām. Sībawayh contrasts completed actions, whose oaths take lām without nūn, and negative oaths, which may retain or omit lā; he cites an unnamed poet's 'fa-lā wa-llāhi tahbiṭu talʿatan' for the negative form. Al-Khalīl treats 'aqsamtu ʿalayka illā faʿalta' and 'lammā faʿalta' as requests modeled on an appeal by God, contrasting the expected positive oath wording 'la-tafʿalunna'."}, {"id": "12:35/q09/p2", "position": "An interrogative environment licenses the emphatic nūn and lām.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash says the clause can host a question like 'which of them will take someone'; a Basran explanation makes an interrogative with ay implicit. The Kufan grammarian allows speech after badā to introduce either an oath or question. Other grammarians object that emphatic nūn would not follow a question such as 'will you stand?'."}, {"id": "12:35/q09/p3", "position": "The heavy emphatic nūn belongs to this form, with different pause and connected forms.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi contrasts the heavy nūn in la-yasjunanna with the light or heavy emphatic nūn in la-yakūnan, and compares the pause form with la-nasfaʿan."}, {"id": "12:35/q09/p4", "position": "The lām is a lām of beginning after badā opens a thought, comparable to constructions with verbs of knowledge and supposition.", "reasons": "Sībawayh compares badā lahum to a thought opened by ẓahara lahum and to ʿalimtu; his examples with ʿalimtu, aẓunnu and Labīd show oath-like lām and nūn in such environments. His separate conditional-oath examples show that a negative response can express future refusal rather than report a past event. Sībawayh cites Labīd's 'la-taʾtiyanna maniyyatī' alongside examples after ʿalima and aẓunnu to show that verbs of knowing and supposing can introduce this oath-like emphatic form."}, {"id": "12:35/q09/p5", "position": "It begins a fresh, independent clause carrying an unspoken oath after badā.", "reasons": "Sībawayh treats 'la-yasjununnahu' as a fresh clause at a point of initiation and uses 'badā lahum ayyuhum afḍal' to show the clause boundary. He reports al-Khalīl's rule that an initial 'la-tafʿalunna' implies an unspoken oath, and applies it to this verse."}]}
{"id": "12:35/q10", "question": "How is the verb 'they will imprison him' alternatively read?", "turns_on": "Whether the resolve is narrated in the third person or voiced as a direct address to the ruler or his group.", "positions": [{"id": "12:35/q10/p1", "position": "With third-person yāʾ: 'they will surely imprison him.'", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi says the third person follows the unseen subject; the written verse has this form. Al-Hasan's alternative addresses the Aziz or his circle."}, {"id": "12:35/q10/p2", "position": "Al-Hasan reads with address tāʾ: 'you will surely imprison him.'", "reasons": "Al-Kashshaf says the address may target the Aziz and those around him, or the Aziz alone deferentially. Al-Baydawi allows people addressing the ruler honorifically or the ruler addressing attendants; Abu Hayyan and al-Samin also give singular or respectful plural possibilities."}]}
{"id": "12:35/q11", "question": "How is 'ḥattā' alternatively read?", "turns_on": "Dialectal substitution of ʿayn for ḥāʾ and Umar's preference for Quraysh recitation.", "positions": [{"id": "12:35/q11/p1", "position": "The ordinary form is ḥattā with ḥāʾ, identified as Quraysh usage.", "reasons": "The report of Umar's letter instructs Ibn Masud to teach Quraysh Arabic after a Hudhayli recitation. Ibn Jinni says the common form is preferable although the other is permissible, since ḥāʾ and ʿayn have close articulation points. Al-Samin says ḥattā marks the endpoint of what precedes."}, {"id": "12:35/q11/p2", "position": "Ibn Masud's Hudhayl form reads ʿattā with ʿayn.", "reasons": "Umar heard this form, asked who had taught it, and wrote Ibn Masud to teach Quraysh usage; al-Durr adds that the Qur'an was revealed in clear Quraysh Arabic. Ibn Jinni explains the consonant exchange by proximity of articulation and allows the variant; al-Kashshaf, Abu Hayyan, al-Samin and al-Alusi identify it as Hudhayl speech."}]}
{"id": "12:35/q12", "question": "What does 'ḥīn' mean as a word?", "turns_on": "Whether ḥīn is taken in its unrestricted lexical range or assigned a length from a particular usage or report.", "positions": [{"id": "12:35/q12/p1", "position": "An indefinite span of time, short or long; the word itself fixes no length.", "reasons": "The linguists in al-Wahidi and al-Razi, Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan, Bursavi and al-Alusi distinguish lexical indefiniteness from estimates of Joseph's actual confinement. Ibn Atiyya says Qur'anic usage supports short and long spans; Abu Hayyan says any specific duration comes from the prison report, not the lexeme. Bursavi says a juristic unqualified oath of 'a while' defaults to six months unless a particular period was meant. Ibn al-Jawzī says ḥīn can be short or long, illustrates a time not yet arrived with poetry, and reports unspecified time in 38:88. He also reports an interpretation of ḥīn in 37:174 as the start of fighting at Badr; this is a comparison from another verse, not an endpoint for Joseph's confinement."}, {"id": "12:35/q12/p2", "position": "It can denote a morning or evening.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas is reported with this lexical possibility. Ibn al-Jawzī reports Qur'anic uses for hours or specified parts of the day in 30:17–18; another report gives midday or the interval between evening prayers in 28:15, which a verifier subsumes under hours."}, {"id": "12:35/q12/p3", "position": "It can denote six months.", "reasons": "Sa'id ibn Jubayr gives this meaning, with Tariq reported to agree; Bursavi says unqualified juristic oaths use six months unless a specific duration was intended. Ibn al-Jawzī reports six months as an exegetical sense of ḥīn in 14:25."}, {"id": "12:35/q12/p4", "position": "It can denote seven years.", "reasons": "Ikrima is reported with this lexical interpretation."}, {"id": "12:35/q12/p5", "position": "It can denote an allotted lifetime or term of enjoyment ending at its appointed limit.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī reports this sense for ḥīn in 2:36, 10:98 and 16:80."}, {"id": "12:35/q12/p6", "position": "It can denote forty years.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī reports this sense for 76:1, while noting that some exegetes include it under unspecified time."}, {"id": "12:35/q12/p7", "position": "It can denote three days.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī reports that some add this sense from the address to Thamud in 51:43."}]}
{"id": "12:35/q13", "question": "What period or endpoint was intended by 'until a time'?", "turns_on": "The verse gives no number; sources differ between the rulers' intended endpoint and reports estimating Joseph's actual stay. Transmissions even vary for Ikrima, al-Kalbi and Muqatil.", "positions": [{"id": "12:35/q13/p1", "position": "No fixed length was stated; they meant an open-ended period, and the exact stay is unknown or only known to have been long.", "reasons":

 "Many commentators leave it unspecified. Ibn Jawzi prefers this because the jailers set no fixed term, while later commentators estimate Joseph's stay. Ibn Ashur says the authorities' words may be open-ended or the narrator omits an irrelevant duration. Al-Razi cites 12:45 for a long imprisonment while declining exactness; al-Alusi similarly avoids choosing a number. Ibn al-Shaykh in Bursavi says the verse only indicates a long stay. Ibn al-Anbari says withholding the period directs people to scholars; Ibn Abi Hatim's report describes the Qur'anic term as unbounded. Al-Aṣamm calls it a long period. Ibn al-Jawzī says this verse itself supplies no endpoint for Joseph's confinement; the endpoint becomes known from his later release. He contrasts another unspecified ḥīn whose endpoint becomes known from the later order to fight."}, {"id": "12:35/q13/p2", "position": "Until city gossip and scandal faded or Joseph's news was forgotten.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas is reported by al-Wahidi, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Alusi; Ata appears in al-Baghawi and Ibn Jawzi. Al-Jubba'i adds that Joseph's news faded. The wife's request and the ruler's apparent goal explain the endpoint."}, {"id": "12:35/q13/p3", "position": "Until the rulers decided what to do with Joseph or observed how he behaved.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari gives a provisional term; Abu Ali reports a decision point; al-Kashshaf, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan connect it to watching Joseph's reaction."}, {"id": "12:35/q13/p4", "position": "One year or thirteen months.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Jawzi report one year, while al-Kiya gives thirteen months; these are distinct estimates of actual duration. Ibn Atiyya relates the estimates to disclosures during Joseph's confinement. Ikrima's vow report gives one year of imprisonment for an unqualified period, but also disallows the promised hand cutting."}, {"id": "12:35/q13/p5", "position": "Six months.", "reasons": "Sa'id ibn Jubayr is named in Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi, with Tariq agreeing in Ibn Abi Hatim."}, {"id": "12:35/q13/p6", "position": "Five years.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbi is named by al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, al-Tabrisi and al-Qurtubi; Ibn Abbas is also reported with five years by al-Wahidi and Ibn Jawzi. Al-Razi, Bursavi and al-Alusi include it among competing estimates. Ibn al-Jawzī reports an unnamed view assigning Joseph five years in prison to 'until a time'."}, {"id": "12:35/q13/p7", "position": "Seven years.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari and Ibn Abi Hatim report Ikrima; al-Wahidi also reports Sufyan, while al-Qurtubi attributes seven to Muqatil. Al-Baydawi states seven; al-Razi, al-Biqa'i, Bursavi and al-Alusi report it among estimates."}, {"id": "12:35/q13/p8", "position": "Nine years.", "reasons": "Al-Tha'labi and al-Qurtubi attribute this estimate to Ikrima, although other sources attribute seven years to him."}, {"id": "12:35/q13/p9", "position": "Ten years.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi reports this from al-Kalbi, while other transmitters give him five years."}, {"id": "12:35/q13/p10", "position": "Twelve years.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi attributes twelve to Muqatil; al-Qurtubi attributes it to Wahb. Al-Razi, Bursavi and al-Alusi include twelve among estimates, and Bursavi says it is the most famous account."}]}
{"id": "12:35/q14", "question": "What does Joseph's imprisonment teach about coercion to commit adultery?", "turns_on": "The degree of coercion: prison threat versus severe beating, and the treatment of sin and penalty.", "positions": [{"id": "12:35/q14/p1", "position": "Threat of imprisonment does not permit adultery, by consensus.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi cites Joseph's refusal despite the threat and his prayer for protection from the women's plot."}, {"id": "12:35/q14/p2", "position": "Under severe beating, the sound view removes the sin of coerced adultery; the claim that its penalty remains is weak.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi distinguishes severe beating from imprisonment and argues from 22:78 that God does not combine two torments."}, {"id": "12:35/q14/p3", "position": "The legal penalty remains even under severe beating.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi reports this claim but calls it weak because God does not combine two torments, citing 22:78."}]}
{"id": "12:35/q15", "question": "How was Joseph publicly taken to prison?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:35/q15/p1", "position": "He was paraded on a donkey through Egypt's markets while a drum and callers announced a false charge against him.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas says the announcement accused the Hebrew of desiring his master and deserving prison; Abu Salih says Ibn Abbas wept whenever recounting the humiliation."}]}
{"id": "12:35/q16", "question": "What did Joseph do during and after imprisonment?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:35/q16/p1", "position": "In prison he comforted, cared for, and interpreted dreams for others, proclaimed his prophetic lineage, and called people to monotheism.", "reasons": "Muqatil gives the acts of care and descent through Jacob, Isaac and Abraham; al-Tabataba'i says prison is where he first identifies his Abrahamic family and teaches monotheism."}, {"id": "12:35/q16/p2", "position": "He refused the king's later summons until his innocence was established and he could leave with his reputation clear.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir links this to 12:50."}, {"id": "12:35/q16/p3", "position": "The baker and cupbearer were also jailed over suspicion of a poisoning plot against the king.", "reasons": "Al-Durr says the baker tried to poison the king and the cupbearer was suspected of collusion."}]}
{"id": "12:35/q17", "question": "Why did God allow Joseph's imprisonment, and what did it reveal?", "turns_on": "The sources give differing theological accounts of divine purpose and human agency, while also recounting human injustice.", "positions": [{"id": "12:35/q17/p1", "position": "God made prison a punishment or expiation for Joseph's earlier inclination toward the woman.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari, al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi state purification from desire. Ibn Abbas counts three lapses: inclination led to prison, asking the cupbearer prolonged it, and accusing the brothers of theft brought their accusation concerning Benjamin; Ibn Atiyya cites 12:24, 12:42, 12:70 and 12:77."}, {"id": "12:35/q17/p2", "position": "God used an unjust prison to protect Joseph's faith, defeat the women's plot, and raise him toward authority.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i says divine power overturns expected causes and establishes Joseph's rank; al-Jishumi's report from al-Asamm says the women gained only his apparent confinement, not religious corruption. Al-Tabataba'i says imprisonment brings him near the king and Egyptian authority. Al-Islahi says Joseph valued faith and character above hardship; Wahb reports Gabriel's message that his resistance through grief, slavery and prison made him among the purified and righteous."}, {"id": "12:35/q17/p3", "position": "The plotting and imprisonment were the people's own acts, not acts created by God.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi states this agency claim even while reporting that the women failed to corrupt Joseph."}, {"id": "12:35/q17/p4", "position": "God caused Joseph's imprisonment, but the account attributes the hardship to the women and his rescue to God, assigning mercy to Him and hardship to them.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān distinguishes divine causation from the narrative's attribution of the imprisonment to the women and rescue to God."}]}
{"id": "12:35/q18", "question": "Was Joseph's earlier prayer a request to be imprisoned?", "turns_on": "Whether the preceding response answers Joseph's request for protection or a supposed request for prison; the later decision wording is the cited test.", "positions": [{"id": "12:35/q18/p1", "position": "No; the response to his prayer was protection from sin, and only afterward did they decide to imprison him.", "reasons": "Al-Tabataba'i uses the sequence of the preceding verse and this verse to reject the claim that God granted a prayer for imprisonment."}, {"id": "12:35/q18/p2", "position": "Yes; the response granted a prayer for imprisonment.", "reasons": "Al-Tabataba'i reports this interpretation only to reject it on the wording of the sequence."}]}
